en: Puggalapaññatti Niddesa 4.
Designation of Fourfold Persons
And what kind of person is an untrue person?

Here, a certain person is a destroyer of life, a taker of what is not given, one who engages in sexual misconduct, a speaker of falsehoods, and one who indulges in fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence—
this is called an untrue person.
And what kind of person is worse than an unvirtuous person?
Here, a certain person himself destroys life and encourages others to destroy life;
he himself takes what is not given and encourages others to take what is not given; he himself engages in sexual misconduct...
Furthermore, one who encourages another in sexual misconduct, who himself speaks falsehood and encourages another in speaking falsehood,
and who himself consumes fermented and distilled liquors that cause heedlessness and encourages another in consuming such liquors—
this person is called "one who is more of an untrue person than an untrue person."
And what kind of person is a true man? Here,

a certain person abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from fermented and distilled liquors that cause negligence—
this is called a "true man."
And what kind of person is more of a true person than a true person?
Here, a certain person refrains from the destruction of life themselves and encourages others in the abstention from the destruction of life;
they refrain from taking what is not given themselves and encourage others in the abstention from taking what is not given.
He himself abstains from sexual misconduct and encourages others to refrain from sexual misconduct;
he himself abstains from false speech and encourages others to refrain from false speech;
he himself abstains from the use of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which cause negligence, and [encourages others to abstain from them].
One encourages another in abstinence—
this person is called "a person more virtuous than a virtuous person.
And what kind of person is wicked?
Here, a certain person is a destroyer of life, a taker of what is not given, one who engages in sexual misconduct,
a speaker of falsehoods, a speaker of divisive speech, a speaker of harsh speech, a speaker of idle chatter, covetous, ill-willed,
and possessed of wrong view.
This person is called "evil.
And what kind of person is more evil than evil?
Here, a certain person himself takes life and also encourages another to take life; he himself...
He himself takes what is not given and encourages others to take what is not given;
he himself engages in sexual misconduct and encourages others to engage in sexual misconduct; he himself speaks falsehood and encourages others to speak falsehood;
he himself speaks divisively and encourages others to speak divisively; he himself speaks harshly...
One is harsh oneself and encourages others in harsh speech; one is a frivolous talker oneself and encourages others in frivolous talk;
one is covetous oneself and encourages others in covetousness; one has a mind of ill will oneself and encourages others in ill will;
one holds wrong view oneself and encourages others in wrong view.
This person is called "one who is more evil than evil.
And what kind of person is virtuous?
Here, a certain person abstains from the destruction of life, abstains from taking what is not given, and abstains from sexual misconduct.
He abstains from taking what is not given, he abstains from false speech, he abstains from malicious speech,
he abstains from harsh speech, he abstains from idle chatter; he is free from covetousness,
he is of a mind without ill will, and he holds right view.
This person is called "virtuous.
And what is the person who is even more virtuous than the virtuous?
Here, a certain person refrains from taking life themselves and encourages others to refrain from taking life.
He encourages others, and he himself abstains from taking what is not given and encourages others in the refraining from taking what is not given;
he himself abstains from sexual misconduct and encourages others in the refraining from sexual misconduct;
he himself abstains from false speech and encourages others in the refraining from false speech; he himself...
He himself abstains from divisive speech and encourages others to refrain from divisive speech;
he himself abstains from harsh speech and encourages others to refrain from harsh speech;
he himself abstains from idle chatter and encourages others to refrain from idle chatter.
One who is themselves free from covetousness and encourages others in freedom from covetousness; who is themselves of a mind without ill will and encourages others in non-ill will;
and who is themselves of right view and encourages others in right view—this person is called "one who is better than the good."
And what kind of person is one of evil nature?
Here, a certain person is a destroyer of life, a taker of what is not given ...
[and so on] ... and holds wrong view.
This person is called one of evil nature.
And what kind of person is more evil-natured than one of evil nature?
Here, a certain person himself destroys life and encourages others to destroy life; he himself takes what is not given and encourages others to take what is not given... [and so on].
One who holds wrong view themselves and encourages others in wrong view—
this person is called "one who is more evil-natured than those of evil nature.
And what kind of person is one of beautiful nature?
Here, a certain person abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, and so forth, up to:
they possess right view—
this person is called "one of beautiful character."
And what kind of person is one who possesses wholesome qualities and is even more wholesome in their qualities?
Here, a certain person refrains from taking life themselves and encourages others in the abstention from taking life; ...
[and so on] ... they possess right view themselves and encourage others in right view.
This person is called one who is "more virtuous in nature than the virtuous.
And what kind of person is blameworthy?
Here, a certain person is endowed with blameworthy bodily action, endowed with blameworthy verbal action, and endowed with blameworthy mental action.
This person is called "blameworthy.
And what kind of person is one who abounds in blameworthiness?
Here, a certain person is endowed largely with blameworthy bodily action and only slightly with blameless [action].
One who is frequently endowed with verbal action that is blameworthy and seldom with that which is blameless;
who is frequently endowed with mental action that is blameworthy and seldom with that which is blameless—
this person is called "one who abounds in blameworthy things."
And what kind of person is one who is rarely blameworthy?
Here, a certain person is endowed mostly with blameless bodily action and little that is blameworthy;
he is endowed mostly with blameless verbal action and little that is blameworthy; he is endowed mostly with... [blameless mental action and little that is blameworthy].
One who is endowed with mental action that is little blameworthy—
this person is called "one of little transgression.
And what kind of person is blameless?
Here, a certain person is endowed with blameless bodily action, endowed with blameless verbal action, and endowed with blameless mental action—
this person is called "blameless.
And what kind of person is one who understands through a condensed statement?
The person for whom the realization of the Dhamma occurs at the very moment it is uttered—
this person is called "one who understands through a brief indication" (ugghaṭitaññū).
And what is the person who understands through elaboration (vipañcitaññū)?
The person for whom, when the meaning of what was spoken in brief is analyzed in detail, there occurs the realization of the Dhamma—
this person is called "one who understands through elaboration" (*vipañcitaññū*).
And what kind of person is "one who must be guided" (*neyya*)?

The person for whom, through recitation, through questioning, through wise attention, and by serving, associating with, and attending upon spiritual friends, there comes about the gradual realization of the Dhamma in this way—
this person is called "one who needs to be guided" (*neyya*).
And what is the person who is "one for whom the words are the limit" (*padaparama*)?
That person who, though hearing much, speaking much, retaining much, and reciting much, does not achieve the realization of the Dhamma in that very life—
this person is called "one for whom words are the limit.
And what kind of person is one who possesses ready wit but not spontaneous wit?
Here, a certain person, when asked a question, speaks appropriately but not quickly;
this person is said to be "one who has appropriate eloquence, but not spontaneous eloquence.
And what kind of person is one who has spontaneous eloquence, but not appropriate eloquence?
Here, a certain person, when asked a question, speaks quickly but not appropriately;
this person is said to be "one who has ready wit but not appropriate wit.
And what kind of person is both one who has appropriate wit and ready wit?
In this case, a certain person, when asked a question, speaks both appropriately and swiftly;
this person is called one who possesses both appropriate and fluent eloquence.
And what kind of person is neither one of appropriate eloquence nor one of fluent eloquence?
Here, a certain person, when questioned with a question, speaks neither appropriately nor swiftly;
this person is called "one who is neither ready-witted nor quick-witted.
In this regard, what are the four types of persons who discourse on the Dhamma?
In this case, a certain Dhamma-preacher speaks little and what he says is disconnected, and his assembly is not skilled in distinguishing what is connected from what is disconnected.
Such a Dhamma-preacher is reckoned merely as a "Dhamma-preacher" among such an assembly.
But in this case, a certain Dhamma-preacher speaks little and what he says is connected, and his assembly is skilled in distinguishing what is connected from what is disconnected.
A Dhamma-preacher of such a kind is reckoned as a "Dhamma-preacher" only by virtue of such an assembly.
But here, some Dhamma-preacher speaks much that is disconnected, and his assembly is not skilled in distinguishing what is connected from what is disconnected.
A Dhamma-preacher of such a kind is reckoned as a "Dhamma-preacher" only by virtue of such an assembly.
Furthermore, here a certain Dhamma-preacher speaks much that is coherent, and his assembly is skilled in distinguishing what is coherent from what is not.
Such a Dhamma-preacher is reckoned as a "Dhamma-preacher" in the presence of such an assembly.
These are the four types of persons who are Dhamma-preachers.
In this regard, who are the four types of persons comparable to clouds? There are four kinds of clouds:
those that thunder but do not rain; those that rain but do not thunder; those that both thunder and rain; and those that neither thunder nor rain.
In the same way, there are these four types of persons resembling clouds found existing in the world.
What are the four?
One who thunders but does not rain; one who rains but does not thunder; one who both thunders and rains; and one who neither thunders nor rains.
And how is a person one who thunders but does not rain?
Here, a certain person is a speaker but not a doer.
In this way, a person is one who thunders but does not rain.
Just as that cloud thunders but does not rain, such is this person.
And how is a person one who rains but does not thunder?
Here, a certain person is a doer, but not a speaker.
In this way, a person is one who rains but does not thunder.
Just as that cloud was one that rained but did not thunder, such is this person.
And how is a person both a thunderer and a rainer?
In this case, a certain person is both a speaker and a doer.
Thus, this person is like one who both thunders and rains;
just as that cloud both thunders and rains, even so is this person.
And how is a person one who neither thunders nor rains?
Here, a certain person is neither a speaker nor a doer.
In this way, a person is one who neither thunders nor rains.
Just as that cloud neither thunders nor rains, such is this person.
These are the four types of persons resembling clouds existing and found in the world.
In this regard, what are the four types of persons resembling mice?
There are four kinds of mice:

one that makes a burrow but does not dwell in it; one that dwells in a burrow but does not make one; one that both makes a burrow and dwells in it; and one that neither makes a burrow nor dwells in one.
In the same way, there are these four types of persons resembling mice existing in the world.
Which four?
One who makes a footing but does not dwell; one who dwells but does not make a footing; one who both makes a footing and dwells; and one who neither makes a footing nor dwells.
And how is a person one who makes a footing but does not dwell?
Here, a certain person masters the Dhamma— the discourses, mixed prose and verse,
expositions, verses, inspired utterances, "thus-it-was-said" passages, birth stories, marvelous qualities, and analytical expositions—
and yet he does not understand, as it really is, "This is suffering," nor does he understand, as it really is, "This is the origin of suffering."
One does not understand as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering," and one does not understand as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, such a person is a maker of a footing, but not a dweller [in the Dhamma].
Just as that mouse was one who made a footing but did not dwell [there], so too is this person.
And how is a person one who dwells but does not make a footing?
Here, a certain person does not master the Dhamma.
Discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, "thus-it-was-said" passages, birth stories, accounts of marvelous phenomena, and analytical expositions.
He understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering";
he understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
One understands it as it truly is.
In this way, such a person is a dweller but not one who makes a firm footing, just like that mouse which was a dweller but did not make a firm footing; this person is comparable to that.
And how is a person one who both digs a deep pit and dwells in it?
Here, a certain person masters the Dhamma—
the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, "thus-it-was-said" passages, birth stories, marvelous qualities, and questions-and-answers.
Thus one understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; one understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering"; one understands as it really is:
"This is the cessation of suffering"; one understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
In this way, a person is both one who makes a footing and one who dwells [therein].
Just as that mouse was both one who made a footing and one who dwelt [therein], so too is this person.
And how is a person neither one who makes a footing nor one who dwells [therein]?

In this case, a certain person does not master the Dhamma— the discourses (sutta), mixed prose and verse (geyya), expositions (veyyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), inspired utterances (udāna), "thus-it-was-said" (itivuttaka), birth stories (jātaka), marvelous qualities (abbhutadhamma), and analytical expositions (vedalla).
He does not understand, as it really is, "This is suffering," nor does he understand, as it really is, "This is the origin of suffering."
One does not understand it as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering," and one does not understand it as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, such a person is neither a maker of a foothold nor an inhabitant.
Just as that mouse neither digs a burrow nor makes a dwelling, so too is this person.
These are the four types of persons resembling mice existing and found in the world.
In this regard, what are the four types of persons resembling mangoes?
There are four kinds of mangoes:

one that is unripe but has the color of the ripe, one that is ripe but has the color of the unripe, one that is unripe and has the color of the unripe, and one that is ripe and has the color of the ripe.
In the same way, there are these four types of persons, comparable to mangoes, existing and found in the world.
Which four?

One who is raw but has the appearance of being ripe; one who is ripe but has the appearance of being raw; one who is raw and has the appearance of being raw; and one who is ripe and has the appearance of being ripe.
And how is a person raw but has the appearance of being ripe?

In this case, a certain person is graceful in advancing and retreating, in looking forward and looking aside, in bending and stretching; he is graceful in carrying his outer robe, bowl, and robes. Yet he does not understand as it really is:
"This is suffering"; he does not understand as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering"; he does not understand as it really is:
"This is the cessation of suffering"; he does not understand as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering."
One does not understand, as it truly is, the path.
In this way, a person is raw but has the appearance of being ripe—just like that mango which is raw but has the appearance of being ripe; such is the likeness of this person.
And how is a person ripe but having the appearance of being unripe?

Here, the way of some person—his advancing and retreating, his looking ahead and looking aside, his bending and stretching, and his manner of carrying the outer robe, bowl, and inner robe—is not inspiring.
Yet he understands as it really is: "This is suffering," and he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering."
“He understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, a person is ripe but has the appearance of being unripe.”
Just as that mango is ripe but has the appearance of being unripe, so too is this person.
And how is a person unripe and having the appearance of being unripe?

Here, a certain person’s advancing and retreating, looking ahead and looking aside, drawing in and extending [the limbs], and the manner of wearing the outer robe, bowl, and inner robes are not graceful.
Thus, one does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering" ... pe ...
nor does one understand as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, a person is unripe and has the appearance of being unripe.
Just as that mango is unripe and has the color of the unripe, so too is this person.
And how is a person ripe and has the color of the ripe?

Here, a certain person is pleasing in his advancing and retreating, in his looking ahead and looking aside, in his drawing in and extending [the limbs], and in his manner of wearing the outer robe, bowl, and inner robe.
Thus he understands as it really is: "This is suffering" ... pe ...
he understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, a person is ripe and possesses the appearance of ripeness.
Just as that mango is ripe and has the color of ripeness, so too is this person.
These are the four types of persons resembling mangoes existing and found in the world.
In this regard, what are the four types of persons resembling jars?
There are four kinds of jars:
one that is empty and covered, one that is full and uncovered, one that is empty and uncovered, and one that is full and covered.
In the same way, there are these four types of persons similar to jars who exist and are found in the world.
Which four?
One who is empty and closed; one who is full and open; one who is empty and open; and one who is full and closed. And how is a person empty and closed?
In this case, a certain person is graceful in advancing and withdrawing, in looking ahead and looking aside, in bending and stretching, and in carrying the outer robe, bowl, and inner robe.
Yet he does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering" ... [and so on] ...
he does not understand as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
In this way, a person is empty and closed off, just like that jar which is empty and closed off; such is this person.
And how is a person full and open?

In this case, for a certain person, his advancing and retreating, his looking forward and looking away, his bending and stretching, and his manner of wearing the outer robe, bowl, and inner robe are not inspiring.
Yet he understands as it really is: "This is suffering" … [and so on] … he understands as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering."
In this way, a person is full and open, just like that jar which is full and open; such is the simile for this person.
And how is a person empty and open?

In this case, for a certain person, his advancing and retreating, his looking forward and looking aside, his bending and stretching, and his manner of wearing the outer robe, bowl, and inner robes are not graceful.
He does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering" ... [and so on] ...
he does not understand as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
In this way, a person is empty and exposed, just like that jar which is empty and exposed; such is the likeness of this person.
And how is a person full and covered?

In this case, there is a certain person whose going forth and returning, looking ahead and looking aside, drawing in and extending [the limbs], and the wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and inner robes are inspiring.
He understands as it really is: "This is suffering" …pe… he understands as it really is:
"This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
In this way, a person is full and covered.
Just as that jar is full and covered, such is the simile for this person.
These are the four types of persons resembling jars who exist and are found in the world.
In this regard, who are the four types of persons comparable to pools of water?
There are four kinds of pools of water:
one that is shallow but appears deep; one that is deep but appears shallow; one that is shallow and appears shallow; and one that is deep and appears deep.
In the same way, there are these four types of persons resembling pools of water existing in the world.
What are the four?
One who is shallow but appears deep; one who is deep but appears shallow; one who is shallow and appears shallow; and one who is deep and appears deep.
And how is a person shallow yet deep in appearance? Here, a certain person’s deportment is pleasing:

his advancing and retreating, looking ahead and looking aside, bending and stretching, and his manner of wearing the outer robe, bowl, and inner robes. Yet he does not understand, as it really is, "This is suffering" ... [and so on] ... ... [as before] ...
[He does not understand, as it really is, "This is the cessation of suffering," "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This is how a person is shallow yet deep in appearance.
“He does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, a person is shallow but appears deep.
Just like that pool of water which is shallow but appears deep, such is this person.”
And how is a person profound yet appearing shallow?

Here, a certain person’s deportment—whether walking forward or backward, looking ahead or looking aside, bending or stretching, and whether in the wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and inner robe—is not inspiring.
Yet he understands as it really is: "This is suffering" ... [and so on].
“He understands as it really is: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, a person is deep but appears shallow.
Just as that pool of water is deep but appears shallow, such is this person.”
And how is a person shallow and of shallow appearance?
Here, a certain person’s manner of advancing and retreating, looking forward and looking aside, drawing in and extending the limbs, and carrying the outer robe, bowl, and upper robe is not inspiring.
He does not understand, as it really is, "This is suffering" ... [and so on] ...
“He does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, such a person is shallow and appears shallow.
Just as that pool of water is shallow and appears shallow, even so is this person.”
And how is a person profound and appearing profound?

Here, a certain person is graceful in his advancing and retreating, in his looking ahead and looking aside, in his bending and stretching, and in his manner of wearing the outer robe, the bowl, and the inner robe.
He understands, as it really is, "This is suffering" … [and so on] … pe … [as above].
“He understands as it really is: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, a person is deep and appears deep.
Just as that lake is deep and appears deep, so too is this person.”
These four types of persons, comparable to pools of water, exist and are found in the world.
In this regard, what are the four types of persons comparable to oxen?
There are four kinds of oxen:

One who is fierce toward his own cattle but not toward the cattle of others; one who is fierce toward the cattle of others but not toward his own cattle; one who is fierce toward both his own cattle and the cattle of others; and one who is fierce neither toward his own cattle nor toward the cattle of others.
In the same way, there are these four types of persons resembling oxen existing in the world.
Which four?

One who is fierce toward his own cattle but not toward others' cattle; one who is fierce toward others' cattle but not toward his own cattle; one who is fierce toward both his own cattle and others' cattle; and one who is neither fierce toward his own cattle nor toward others' cattle.
And how is a person fierce toward his own cattle but not toward others' cattle?
Here, a certain person causes alarm in his own assembly, but not in another's assembly.
Thus, a person is fierce toward his own cattle but not toward the cattle of others.
Just as that ox is fierce toward its own cattle but not toward the cattle of others, such is this person.
And how is a person fierce toward the cattle of others but not toward his own cattle?
In this case, a certain person is one who intimidates the assemblies of others, but not his own assembly.
Thus, such a person is fierce toward the cattle of others, but not fierce toward his own cattle.
Just as that ox is fierce toward the cattle of others but not fierce toward its own cattle, even so is this person.
And how is a person fierce toward his own cattle and fierce toward the cattle of others?
Here, a certain person causes agitation both in his own assembly and in the assembly of others.
In this way, a person is fierce toward his own cattle and fierce toward the cattle of others.
Just as that ox is fierce toward its own cattle and fierce toward the cattle of others, so too is this person.
And how is a person neither fierce toward its own cattle nor fierce toward the cattle of others?
Here, a certain person does not cause agitation in his own assembly, nor does he cause agitation in the assembly of others.
In this way, a person is neither fierce toward his own cattle nor fierce toward the cattle of others.
Just as that ox is neither fierce toward its own cattle nor fierce toward the cattle of others, such is this person.
These are the four types of persons resembling oxen who exist and are found in the world.
In this regard, who are the four types of persons comparable to venomous snakes? There are four kinds of venomous snakes:

one whose venom has been activated but is not virulent; one whose venom is virulent but has not been activated; one whose venom has both been activated and is virulent; and one whose venom has neither been activated nor is virulent.
In the same way, there are these four types of persons resembling venomous snakes existing in the world.
Which four?
One whose venom is slow-acting but not fierce; one whose venom is fierce but not slow-acting; one whose venom is both slow-acting and fierce; and one whose venom is neither slow-acting nor fierce.
And how is a person one whose venom is swift-acting but not long-lasting?
Here, a certain person becomes angry frequently;
yet that anger of his does not persist for a long time.
In this way, a person has poison that has come forth, but is not virulent.
Just as that viper has poison that has come forth but is not virulent, so too is this person.
And how does a person have virulent poison, but it has not come forth?
In this case, there is a certain person who does not become angry frequently;
yet his anger persists for a long time, for many nights.
In this way, such a person is one whose venom is terrible, but whose venom is not quick-acting.
Just as that venomous snake is fierce in its venom but has not yet released it, such is this person.
And how is a person both one who has released the venom and one who is fierce in its venom?
Here, a certain person becomes angry frequently.
And his anger persists for a long time, throughout a vast period.
Thus, this person is one whose venom has arrived and whose venom is terrible.
Just as that viper is one whose venom has arrived and whose venom is terrible, even so is this person.
And how is a person one whose venom is neither arrived nor fierce?
Here, a certain person does not frequently become angry;
moreover, that anger of his does not persist for a long time.
In this way, such a person is neither one whose venom has been provoked nor one whose venom is fierce.
Just as that viper is neither one whose venom has been provoked nor one whose venom is fierce, even so is this person.
These are the four types of persons comparable to vipers who exist and are found in the world.
And how does a person, without investigating and without scrutinizing, speak in praise of one who deserves censure? Here,
a certain person speaks in praise of those who have practiced wrongly, who have practiced erroneously— the sectarian teachers and the disciples of sectarian teachers—
saying, "They have practiced well," and "They have practiced rightly."

In this way, a person speaks in praise of one who does not deserve praise, without having investigated or scrutinized the matter. And how does a person speak in dispraise of one who deserves praise, without having investigated or scrutinized the matter? Here, a certain person speaks in dispraise of those Buddhas and disciples of the Buddha who have practiced well and practiced rightly: [He says: "Those Blessed Ones, the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, are not truly Arahants, they are not truly Perfectly Enlightened Ones; their Dhamma is not well-proclaimed, it is not conducive to peace, it is not conducive to enlightenment, it is not conducive to nibbāna; these disciples of the Blessed One are not well-practiced, they are not practicing rightly; they are not walking the path of the true Dhamma, they do not attain the fruits of the holy life, they do not realize the supreme security from bondage that is nibbāna. Thus, a person speaks in dispraise of those who deserve praise, without having investigated or scrutinized the matter. This is called a person who speaks in dispraise of those who deserve praise, without having investigated or scrutinized the matter. Furthermore, a person speaks in dispraise of those who deserve praise, without having investigated or scrutinized the matter, when he speaks in dispraise of the Buddhas and their disciples who have practiced well and practiced rightly, saying: "These Blessed Ones, the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, are not truly Arahants, they are not truly Perfectly Enlightened Ones; their Dhamma is not well-proclaimed, it is not conducive to peace, it is not conducive to enlightenment, it is not conducive to nibbāna; these disciples of the Blessed One are not well-practiced, they are not practicing rightly; they are not walking the path of the true Dhamma, they do not attain the fruits of the holy life, they do not realize the supreme security from bondage that is nibbāna. This too is called a person who speaks in dispraise of those who deserve praise, without having investigated or scrutinized the matter. Furthermore, a person speaks in dispraise of those who deserve praise, without having investigated or scrutinized the matter, when he speaks in dispraise of the Buddhas and their disciples who have practiced well and practiced rightly, saying: "These Blessed Ones, the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, are not truly Arahants, they are not truly Perfectly Enlightened Ones; their Dhamma is not well-proclaimed, it is not conducive to peace, it is not conducive to enlightenment, it is not conducive to nibbāna; these disciples of the Blessed One are not well-practiced, they are not practicing rightly; they are not walking the path of the true Dhamma, they do not attain the fruits of the holy life, they do not realize the supreme security from bondage that is nibbāna. He speaks that which is a quality worthy of praise there, truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time; he does not speak that which is a quality unworthy of praise there, even though it is truthful, accurate, and timely.

In this way, a person speaks praise of one who deserves praise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time—but does not speak dispraise of one who deserves dispraise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time.

He knows the right occasion for answering that question.

Thus, this person speaks dispraise of one who deserves dispraise as it truly is, as it really is, and at the proper time, and he speaks praise of one who deserves praise as it truly is, as it really is, and at the proper time.

He does not speak the dispraise that exists there, truthful and correct, at the proper time; nor does he speak the praise that exists there, truthful and correct, at the proper time.
He dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
Such a person neither speaks dispraise at the proper time of one who deserves dispraise—truthful and correct—nor speaks praise at the proper time of one who deserves praise—truthful and correct.
And what kind of person is one who subsists on the fruit of exertion, but does not subsist on the fruit of merit?
The person for whom livelihood is produced through exerting, striving, and endeavoring, but not from merit—
this person is called one who lives on the fruit of exertion, not on the fruit of merit.
And what kind of person lives on the fruit of merit, but not on the fruit of exertion?
Starting from the gods who wield power over the creations of others (Paranimmitavasavatti), the gods above them subsist on the fruit of merit; they do not subsist on the fruit of exertion.
And what kind of person subsists both on the fruit of exertion and on the fruit of merit?
It is the person for whom livelihood is produced through exerting, striving, and endeavoring, as well as from merit.
This person is said to be "one who lives on the fruit of exertion and one who lives on the fruit of merit.
And what kind of person is neither one who lives on the fruit of exertion nor one who lives on the fruit of merit?
Those in hell are neither those who live on the fruit of exertion nor those who live on the fruit of merit.
And how is a person "dark with a dark destination"?
Here, a certain person is reborn into a low family—

a family of outcasts (caṇḍāla), or hunters (nesāda), or bamboo-workers (vena), or chariot-makers (rathakāra), or waste-removers (pukkusa)— one that is poor, lacking food and drink, living in hardship, where even basic sustenance and clothing are obtained only with great difficulty.
And he is ugly, unsightly, deformed, and afflicted with many ailments—perhaps blind, or crooked, or lame, or paralyzed;
he does not obtain food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, bedding, dwellings, or lamps.
He engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind.

Thus, having practiced misconduct by way of body, having practiced misconduct by way of speech, and having practiced misconduct by way of mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
In this way, a person is dark with a dark destiny.
And how is a person dark with a bright destiny?
In this case, a certain person is reborn into a low family—

such as a family of scavengers, hunters, bamboo-workers, cartwrights, or waste-removers— a family that is poor, lacking food and drink, and living in hardship, where even basic sustenance is obtained with great difficulty.
Furthermore, he is ugly, unsightly, deformed, afflicted by many diseases, or is one-eyed, crippled, lame, or paralyzed.
Or, he does not obtain food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, bedding, dwellings, or lighting.
Yet, he practices good conduct with the body, he practices good conduct with speech, and he practices good conduct with the mind.

Having practiced good conduct with the body, having practiced good conduct with speech, and having practiced good conduct with the mind, at the breaking up of the body after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
Thus is a person who is dark but destined for light.
And how is a person who is bright but destined for darkness?
Here, a certain person is reborn into a high family—

He is born into a great khattiya clan, or a great brahmin clan, or a great householder clan—wealthy, with great riches and vast enjoyments, possessing abundant gold and silver, abundant assets and requisites, and abundant wealth and grain.

And he is handsome, beautiful, pleasing, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion, and a recipient of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps.
Thus, one engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind.

Having engaged in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even hell.
In this way, such a person is bright but has a dark future destiny.
And how is a person a light whose destiny is light?
Here, a certain person is reborn into a high family—

a prominent khattiya family, a prominent brahmin family, or a prominent householder family— one that is wealthy, of great fortune and great possessions, with abundant gold and silver, abundant wealth and equipment, and abundant money and grain.

And he is handsome, beautiful, pleasing, endowed with the supreme excellence of complexion; he is a recipient of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps.
He practices good conduct by body, he practices good conduct by speech, and he practices good conduct by mind.

Having practiced good conduct by body, having practiced good conduct by speech, and having practiced good conduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
In this way, a person is bright and has brightness as his destination.

… [as before] … in this way a person is one who bends down and rises up. And how is a person one who rises up and bends down? … [as before] … in this way a person is one who rises up and bends down.

Thus a person is one who rises and falls.
In this regard, who are the four types of persons comparable to trees? There are four kinds of trees:
one that is softwood with a heartwood surround; one that is heartwood with a softwood surround; one that is softwood with a softwood surround; and one that is heartwood with a heartwood surround.
In the same way, there are these four types of persons comparable to trees found existing in the world.
Which four?
One who is softwood with a heartwood retinue; one who is heartwood with a softwood retinue; one who is softwood with a softwood retinue; and one who is heartwood with a heartwood retinue.
And how is a person softwood with a heartwood retinue?
Here, a certain person is immoral and of evil character, yet his assembly is virtuous and of good character.
In this way, a person is softwood with a heartwood retinue.
Just as that tree has softwood surrounded by heartwood, so too is this person.
And how is a person heartwood with softwood surrounding it?
Here, a certain person is virtuous and of good character, yet his retinue is unvirtuous and of evil character.
Thus, a person is like heartwood surrounded by sapwood.
Just as that tree has heartwood surrounded by sapwood, so too is this person.
And how is a person sapwood surrounded by sapwood?
In this case, a certain person is immoral and of evil character, and his retinue is also immoral and of evil character.
Thus, that person is like softwood with a retinue of softwood.
Just as that tree is softwood with a retinue of softwood, so too is this person.
And how is a person essential with an essential retinue?
Here, a certain person is virtuous and of good character, and his assembly is also virtuous and of good character.
In this way, a person is essential with an essential retinue.
Just as that tree has heartwood and is surrounded by heartwood, even so is this person.
These are the four types of persons comparable to trees existing and found in the world.
And what kind of person is one who takes form as the measure and finds satisfaction in form?

In this case, a certain person, having seen the height, or having seen the circumference, or having seen the shape, or having seen the fullness [of a form], takes it as a measure and conceives confidence therein.
This person is called one who has the measure of form and is confident in form.
And what kind of person is one who has the measure of sound and is confident in sound?
Here, a certain person, having taken the measure of another’s praise, another’s laudation, another’s eulogy, or another’s commendation, generates confidence therein.
This person is called one who has the sound as his measure and is confident in the sound.
And what kind of person is one who has the coarse as his measure and is confident in the coarse?

Here, a certain person, upon seeing the coarseness of robes, or the coarseness of the alms-bowl, or the coarseness of lodgings, or various forms of ascetic practice, takes them as a measure and conceives faith therein.
This person is called one who takes the coarse as his measure and has faith in what is coarse.
And what kind of person is one who takes the Dhamma as his measure and has faith in the Dhamma?
In this case, a certain person, having seen virtue, or having seen concentration, or having seen wisdom, takes them as a measure and conceives confidence therein.
This person is called one who has the Dhamma as his measure and is confident in the Dhamma.
And how does a person practice for his own welfare but not for the welfare of others?
In this case, a certain person is himself accomplished in virtue, but does not encourage others in the accomplishment of virtue;
he is himself accomplished in concentration, but does not encourage others in the accomplishment of concentration;
he is himself accomplished in wisdom, but does not encourage others in the accomplishment of wisdom.
One is oneself accomplished in liberation, but does not encourage others to achieve accomplishment in liberation;
one is oneself accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation, but does not encourage others to achieve accomplishment in the knowledge and vision of liberation.
In this way, such a person is practicing for their own benefit, but not for the benefit of others.
And how does a person practice for the benefit of others but not for their own benefit?
Here, a certain person is themselves not accomplished in virtue, yet they encourage another in the accomplishment of virtue;
they are themselves not accomplished in concentration, yet they encourage another in the accomplishment of concentration.
He himself is not perfected in wisdom, yet he encourages others in the perfection of wisdom;
he himself is not perfected in liberation, yet he encourages others in the perfection of liberation;
he himself is not perfected in the knowledge and vision of liberation, yet he encourages others in the perfection of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
In this way, a person practices for the benefit of others but not for their own benefit.
And how does a person practice both for their own benefit and for the benefit of others?
Here, a certain person is themselves accomplished in virtue and encourages others in the accomplishment of virtue.
One is oneself accomplished in concentration and encourages others in the accomplishment of concentration;
one is oneself accomplished in wisdom and encourages others in the accomplishment of wisdom;
one is oneself accomplished in liberation and encourages others in the accomplishment of liberation.
One is oneself endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation, and one encourages another in the attainment of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
In this way, a person is practicing both for their own benefit and for the benefit of others.
And how does a person practice neither for their own benefit nor for the benefit of others?
In this case, a certain person is not himself accomplished in virtue, nor does he encourage others in the accomplishment of virtue;
he is not himself accomplished in concentration, nor does he encourage others in the accomplishment of concentration;
he is not himself accomplished in wisdom, nor does he encourage others in the accomplishment of wisdom.
One is not oneself accomplished in liberation, nor does one encourage others in the accomplishment of liberation;
one is not oneself accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation, nor does one encourage others in the accomplishment of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Thus, such a person is practicing neither for their own benefit nor for the benefit of others.
And how is a person one who torments themselves, devoted to the practice of self-torment?
Here, a certain person goes naked, rejecting conventions, licking his hands; he does not come when asked, nor does he stay when asked;
he accepts nothing brought to him, nothing specially prepared for him, nor an invitation; he does not accept food from the mouth of a pot.
He does not accept [food] from the mouth of a basket; nor from between sheep, nor between a staff, nor between a pestle;
nor from two people eating together; nor from a pregnant woman, nor from a woman nursing, nor from a woman in her courses;
nor from crowds; nor where she is standing in attendance, nor where flies are swarming; nor fish, nor meat.
He drinks neither fermented liquor, nor spirits, nor grain-beer.
He is either a "one-house" man or a "one-morsel" man, or he is a "two-house" man or a "two-morsel" man...
[and so on] ...or he is a "seven-house" man or a "seven-morsel" man.
He subsists on one morsel of food, or he subsists on two morsels of food …pe… or he subsists on seven morsels of food;
he takes food once a day, or he takes food once every two days …pe…
He takes food once every seven days.
Thus, he dwells devoted to the practice of taking meals at intervals, even for as long as half a month.
He becomes one who eats greens, or one who eats millet, or one who eats wild rice, or one who eats coarse grain.

He eats only once a day, or he eats at every fourth mealtime, or he eats at every seventh mealtime, or he eats at every fifteenth mealtime, or he eats at every thirtieth mealtime, or he eats at every forty-fifth mealtime;
or he subsists on what grows wild, or he eats only fallen fruit. He lives on forest roots and fruits, consuming only what has been dropped.
He wears hemp garments, or he wears flaxen garments, or he wears rags from a cemetery, or he wears robes made of discarded cloth.
He wears garments of tirīṭa grass; he wears deerskins; he wears a cloak made of pieces of deerskin; he wears a garment of kusa grass; he wears a garment of bark;
he wears a garment of wood-shavings; he wears a blanket of human hair; he wears a blanket of animal wool; he wears a cloak of owls' wings;
he becomes one who pulls out his hair and beard, devoted to the practice of pulling out his hair and beard; he becomes one who stands continuously.
He rejects sitting down; he remains in a squatting posture, devoted to the exertion of squatting;
he uses a bed of thorns, spreading his sleep upon a bed of thorns; and he dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water three times a day.
Thus, in such ways, he dwells engaged in various kinds of bodily mortification and self-torment.
In this way, a person is one who torments themselves and is devoted to the practice of self-torment.
And how is a person one who torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others?

Here, a certain person is a butcher of sheep, a butcher of pigs, a fowler, a hunter, a trapper, a fisherman, a thief, an executioner, a butcher of cattle, a jailer, or anyone else engaged in cruel occupations.
In this way, a person is one who torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
And how is a person one who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of tormenting himself, as well as one who torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others?
Here, a certain person is either a consecrated Kṣatriya king or a wealthy Brāhmaṇa.
Thus, having had a new assembly hall built to the east of the city, having shaved off his hair and beard, having put on a rough antelope skin,
and having anointed his body with ghee and oil, he entered the assembly hall together with his chief queen and the brahmin family priest, scratching his back with a deer horn.
Thus, he makes his bed there on the bare ground smeared with green cow dung.
A cow that has a calf of the same color provides the milk from one udder for the king’s sustenance;
the milk from the second udder provides for the chief queen’s sustenance; the milk from the third udder...
With that [milk], he sustains the brahmin household priest; with the milk that remains from the fourth portion, he offers oblations to the fire;
and with what is left over, the calf is sustained.
He speaks thus:
“Let so many bulls be slain for the sake of sacrifice; let so many young oxen be slain for the sake of sacrifice;
let so many heifers be slain for the sake of sacrifice; let so many goats be slain for the sake of sacrifice; let so many sheep be slain for the sake of sacrifice;
let so many horses be slain for the sake of sacrifice; let so many trees be cut down for the sake of sacrificial posts.”
"Let this much grass be cut for the purpose of making a sacrificial bed.
And those who are his slaves, messengers, or laborers—they too perform their services while driven by the threat of punishment and the fear of danger, weeping with tearful faces.
Thus, such a person is one who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment, and he is one who torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
And how is a person neither one who torments himself nor is devoted to the practice of tormenting himself, neither one who torments others nor is devoted to the practice of tormenting others?
He, neither tormenting himself nor tormenting others, in this very life is free from craving, extinguished, become cool, experiencing happiness, and dwells with a self that has become sublime.

Here, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.

Thus, having realized for himself through direct higher knowledge this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its princes and people, he makes it known.
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
A householder, or a householder’s son, or one born into some other family hears that Dhamma.
Having heard that Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata.
Possessed of that attainment of faith, he reflects thus:
"Household life is crowded and dusty; going forth is the open air."
"It is not easy for one living in a household to lead the holy life in its complete perfection, in its total purity, polished like a conch shell.
What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?
After some time, he abandoned his mass of wealth—whether small or great—and went forth.

Having abandoned a small circle of relatives or having abandoned a large circle of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on saffron-colored robes, and goes forth from the household life into homelessness.

Having thus gone forth, having entered upon the training and way of life of the bhikkhus, he abandons the taking of life and abstains from taking life; he lays aside the rod and the weapon, and dwells conscientious, compassionate, and sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings.
Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and dwells with a heart free from theft and pure.
Having abandoned unchastity, he lives a life of chastity; he dwells aloof and abstains from sexual intercourse, the common practice of the village.
Having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech; he speaks the truth, is devoted to truth, is trustworthy, reliable, and not a deceiver of the world.

Having abandoned malicious speech, he abstains from malicious speech. Having heard something here, he does not repeat it elsewhere for the purpose of dividing these people; nor, having heard something elsewhere, does he repeat it here for the purpose of dividing those people.

Thus, he is a reconciler of those who are divided and a promoter of harmony among those who are united. Delighting in concord, rejoicing in concord, finding joy in concord, he speaks words that bring about concord.
Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech.
He speaks such speech as is blameless, pleasing to the ear, affectionate, heart-moving, urbane, agreeable to many people, and dear to many people.

Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma, speaks on the Vinaya; he utters speech that is worth treasuring, timely, reasoned, measured, and connected with the goal.
He abstains from damaging seeds and plants; he eats only once a day, refraining from eating at night and abstaining from food outside the proper time.

He abstains from eating at improper times; he abstains from attending dances, songs, music, and theatrical spectacles; he abstains from wearing garlands, scents, unguents, and from the use of ornaments and finery;
he abstains from high and luxurious beds and seats; he abstains from accepting gold and silver;
he abstains from accepting raw grain; he abstains from accepting raw meat; he abstains from accepting women and girls.
He abstains from accepting male and female slaves; he abstains from accepting goats and sheep;
he abstains from accepting chickens and pigs; he abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares;
he abstains from accepting fields and land; he abstains from engaging in the practice of acting as a messenger or an envoy.
He abstains from buying and selling; he abstains from false weights, false metals, and false measures; he abstains from bribery, deception, and fraud;
he abstains from mutilation, murder, abduction, robbery, and violence.
He is content with robes to protect his body and almsfood to sustain his belly.

Thus, wherever he goes, he goes taking only what is necessary; just as a winged bird flies with its wings as its only burden, even so a bhikkhu is content with robes to protect his body and almsfood to sustain his belly.
Wherever he goes, he goes taking only these things.
Thus, endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, he experiences within himself the happiness of blamelessness.
Having seen a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary details.
For, if he were to dwell with this faculty of the eye unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might arise.

If, when he has seen a form with the eye, there should arise in him states that are covetous and deplorable, states that lead to bondage, then he practices for its restraint, guards the faculty of the eye, and attains restraint over the faculty of the eye;
having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose... [and so on].
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue … having touched a tangible object with the body … having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind,
one does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
Since, if he were to dwell with this faculty of mind unguarded, covetousness and dejection— evil, unwholesome states— might flow in upon him,
he practices for its restraint, guards the faculty of mind, and attains restraint over the faculty of mind.
Possessed of this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences within himself the unsullied happiness.
Thus, he acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside;
he acts with clear comprehension when bending and stretching his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing his outer robe, inner robe, and bowl;
he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension when defecating and urinating.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, or remaining silent,
he acts with clear comprehension. Endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, endowed with this noble restraint of the sense faculties,
endowed with this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension, and endowed with this noble contentment—

Endowed with this, he resorts to a secluded lodging: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, or an open space under the sky, or a heap of straw.
Having returned from his almsround after his meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Thus, having abandoned covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness.
Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate and sympathetic toward all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill will and hatred.
Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind of sloth and torpor.
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells unagitated, with a mind inwardly calmed; he purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse.
Having abandoned doubt, he dwells as one who has crossed beyond doubt, free from uncertainty regarding wholesome states; he purifies his mind of doubt.
Having abandoned these five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—he, quite secluded from sensual pleasures...
Secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

With the subsiding of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and mental unification, is without thought and examination, and possesses rapture and happiness born of concentration.
With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending;
he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: “He dwells happily, mindful and equanimous”; thus he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
He recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say:
one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births...
Twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births,
a hundred thousand births; many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, and many aeons of both world-contraction and expansion—
“In that place I was with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan; passing away from there, I arose elsewhere.
There too I was with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan; passing away from there, I reappeared here.
Thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes and details.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.

“Indeed, these worthy beings were possessed of misconduct of body, possessed of misconduct of speech, and possessed of misconduct of mind; they were revilers of the noble ones, holders of wrong view, and undertakers of actions based on wrong view.
With the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.”

"Or else, these worthy beings were endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, and endowed with good conduct of mind; they did not revile the noble ones, held right view, and undertook actions based on right view.
With the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a happy destination, a heavenly world.

Thus, with the purified divine eye, surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—lowly and exalted, beautiful and ugly, in happy destinations and unhappy destinations—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
He understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering";
he understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering."
One understands as it really is: "These are the taints"; one understands as it really is: "This is the origin of the taints"; one understands as it really is:
"This is the cessation of the taints"; one understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints."
One understands it as it truly is.
For one who knows thus and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensuality, the mind is liberated from the influx of existence, and the mind is liberated from the influx of ignorance.
When it is liberated, there is the knowledge: "It is liberated."
“He understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
Thus, that person neither torments himself nor is devoted to the practice of self-torment, and neither torments others nor is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
Being neither a tormentor of self nor a tormentor of others, he dwells in this very life—free from hunger, extinguished, become cool, experiencing bliss, with a self that has become sublime.”
And what kind of person is one with lust?
That person whose lust has not been abandoned—this is called a person "with lust.
And what kind of person is one with hatred?
The person whose hatred has not been abandoned is called a person "with hatred.
And what is the person with delusion?
The person whose delusion has not been abandoned is called a person "with delusion."
And what kind of person is one who is conceited?
That person whose conceit has not been abandoned is called a "conceited" person.
And how is a person one who attains internal tranquility of mind but does not attain higher wisdom and insight into phenomena?
In this case, a certain person is an attainer of meditative attainments (samāpatti) associated with the form realm or the formless realm, but is not an attainer of the supramundane path or its fruit.
Thus, a person is an attainer of internal mental tranquility (cetosamatha), but not an attainer of higher wisdom through insight into phenomena (adhipaññādhammavipassanā).
And how is a person an attainer of higher wisdom through insight into phenomena, but not an attainer of internal mental tranquility?

In this case, a certain person is an attainer of the supramundane path or its fruit, but is not an attainer of the meditative attainments (samāpatti) associated with the form realm or the formless realm.
Likewise, a person may be an attainer of higher wisdom and insight into phenomena (adhipaññādhammavipassanā), but not an attainer of internal mental tranquility (ajjhattaṃ cetosamatha).
And how does a person become both an attainer of internal mental tranquility and an attainer of higher wisdom and insight into phenomena?
In this case, a certain person is an attainer of meditative attainments (samāpatti) accompanied by the form realm or the formless realm, or an attainer of the supramundane path or its fruit.
In this way, such a person is both an attainer of internal mental serenity (cetosamatha) and an attainer of higher wisdom consisting in insight into phenomena (adhipaññādhammavipassanā).
And how is a person neither an attainer of internal mental serenity nor an attainer of higher wisdom consisting in insight into phenomena?

Here, a certain person is neither an attainer of meditative attainments (samāpatti) associated with the form realm nor those associated with the formless realm, nor is he an attainer of the supramundane path or its fruit.
In this way, such a person is neither an attainer of internal mental tranquility (cetosamatha) nor an attainer of higher wisdom through insight into phenomena (adhipaññādhammavipassanā).
And what kind of person is one who goes with the stream (anusotagāmī)?
Here, a certain person indulges in sensual pleasures and performs evil deeds.
This person is called "one who goes with the stream.
And what kind of person is one who goes against the stream?
Here, a certain person does not indulge in sensual pleasures and does not perform evil deeds.
Even with pain and even with mental distress, even weeping with a tearful face, he leads the holy life (brahmacariya) in its full perfection and purity.
This person is called "one who goes against the stream."
And what kind of person is one who is "steadfast in self"?
Here, a certain person, through the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, no longer subject to returning from that world.
This is called a person who is "steadfast in self."
And what kind of person is the brahmin who has crossed over, gone to the further shore, and stands on firm ground?

Here, a certain person, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it.
This is called the person who has crossed over, gone to the further shore, and stands on firm ground—a brahmin.
And how is a person one who has heard little and is not established in what he has heard?
Here, a certain person has heard little—sutta, geyya, veyyākaraṇa, gāthā, udāna, itivuttaka, jātaka, abbhutadhamma, and vedalla.
Yet, having failed to understand the meaning and the Dhamma of that little he has heard, he does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
In this way, a person is of little learning and has not mastered what he has heard.
And how is a person of little learning yet has mastered what he has heard?
Here, a certain person has heard only a little—sutta, geyya, veyyākaraṇa, gāthā, udāna, itivuttaka, jātaka, abbhutadhamma, and vedalla—but he has mastered it.
Thus, having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma of that little he has heard, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma and its progressive sequence.
In this way, a person is one who has heard little but is established in what he has heard.
And how is a person one who has heard much but is not established in what he has heard?
In this case, a certain person has heard much—suttas, geyyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, itivuttakas, jātakas, abbhutadhammas, and vedallas.
Yet, having failed to understand the meaning and the Dhamma of that extensive learning, he does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
In this way, a person is "learned" but has not attained through his learning.
And how is a person one who has heard much and is established in what has been heard?
Here, a certain person has heard much—the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, legends, birth stories, marvelous qualities, and analyses.
Having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma of that great amount of learning, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma.
In this way, a person is one who has heard much and is established in what has been heard.
And what is the person who is an unshakable ascetic?

Here, a certain person, through the complete destruction of three fetters, becomes a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and having enlightenment as his final goal.
This person is called a "steadfast ascetic" (*samaṇamacala*).
And what kind of person is a "lotus-like ascetic" (*samaṇapaduma*)?

Here, a certain person, through the complete destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, becomes a once-returner; having returned to this world only once more, he makes an end of suffering.
This person is called a "lotus-like ascetic" (*samaṇapaduma*).
And what kind of person is a "white-lotus-like ascetic" (*samaṇapuṇḍarīka*)?

Here, a certain person, through the complete destruction of the five lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*), becomes one of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*), attaining final nibbāna there, no longer subject to returning from that world.
This person is called a "white-lotus ascetic" (*samaṇapuṇḍarīka*).
And what kind of person is a "delicate ascetic among ascetics" (*samaṇesu samaṇasukhumāla*)?

Here, a certain person, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon them.
This person is called "a delicate ascetic among ascetics.
This concludes the Exposition of the Tetrads.
